text:
**OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman** joins Alex Kantrowitz to describe OpenAI’s path from conversational ChatGPT toward a persistent personal AGI: an agent that takes goals, maintains context, uses tools, and acts on the user’s behalf with minimal interface. He argues that model capability, compute scarcity, trust, and real-world value (especially in health) will shape who wins, while pricing, competition, and ecosystems evolve around rising demand rather than pure commoditization.

**From chat to agents and a vanishing interface**
- Brockman frames the goal as AGI, not a “super app.” Early ChatGPT was a language model without memory, tools, or lasting context; the destination is an AI that continually works for the user—organizing inboxes, pursuing health plans, solving hard and mundane problems.
- Ideal interaction is almost no product UI: talk to a persistent entity the way people talk to each other. OpenAI is unifying ChatGPT, browser/computer control, and Codex-style agents so users stop switching modes and clicking toggles.
- Agents already act: Codex (despite the name) is a general tool-using harness. Non-technical OpenAI staff hook it to Slack, Gmail, and calendars; one comms colleague used it to collect dietary preferences and build a seating chart. ChatGPT will increasingly suggest next steps and then execute them (draft/send emails, book specialists) once the user agrees, with permission levels that scale with earned trust.
- Early plugins (2023) failed because models were too weak and context too small. Today models handle many tools, large contexts, and hard math/physics problems, so agents are becoming practical across engineering, finance, legal, sales, and personal life.

**Ecosystem, “operating system,” and devices**
- Brockman expects a vibrant partner ecosystem: companies often welcome OpenAI training models to use their software because usage rises. Shutting AI out risks decline.
- He resists calling ChatGPT a classic OS; it is the natural interface to personal AGI—an assistant with its own computer plus delegated access to the user’s systems, analogous to a human coworker with clear trust boundaries.
- On Apple/Siri and hardware: new capability eras rewrite interfaces. Public reports and prior comments confirm OpenAI device work, but Brockman stresses the agentic form factor and continuous context (meetings, evolving business processes) over any single gadget. Devices are interfaces to the agent, not the agent itself.
- Voice should become fluid and bidirectional—overlapping speech, interruption, simultaneous listen/speak—rather than rigid turn-taking chained STT–LLM–TTS pipelines. Voice already feels magical for commutes and Codex feedback but breaks when the system talks over the user; natural conversation is a major target for work and life.

**Model progress, differentiation, and compute**
- Scaling has not hit a wall. Internally, apparent stalls usually trace to bugs or implementation gaps. Decades of neural-net history track compute; fundamentals still allow progress though building giant clusters is hard and expensive (custom network protocols, full-stack debugging).
- Intelligence is multi-dimensional. Raw capability matters, but domain expertise (pitches, spreadsheets, science) requires prioritization; depth in a field unlocks more problems (AlphaGo’s move 37 as analogy). Room remains for differentiation even if many labs scale.
- Compute is the binding constraint: demand will outstrip supply as agents reach planetary scale and deeper usage. OpenAI’s stance has been to buy “all of it,” invest years ahead (including its own chip effort), and treat meeting economic demand as the core challenge. Growth and willingness to pay support the spend; the economy-wide upside is still under-appreciated.

**Pricing, enterprises, and competition**
- OpenAI has long raised intelligence while cutting price for a given capability level. Frontier stays premium; yesterday’s frontier becomes cheap. No expectation of a sudden massive short-term price collapse, but a year-out view of today’s top tier will be far more affordable while a new frontier appears.
- Enterprises have shifted from FOMO to ROI, spend controls, and observability—tools OpenAI is shipping. The market and OpenAI’s revenue ramp are still early and steep.
- On Satya Nadella’s “models are a commodity / company-specific systems win” framing and Microsoft dynamics: Brockman says no layer (compute, models, domain systems) drops out of the value chain; they multiply. Compute is not truly commoditized under scarcity; smarter models uniquely accelerate science; domain workflows and regulation still need specialized builders. He focuses on AI transforming the economy and welcomes others doing the same rather than dwelling on rivalry. He declines to confirm GPT-5.6 rumors beyond “better, faster, smarter.”

**Health as a flagship use case**
- Brockman says standout stories (e.g., intensive personal diagnostics fed into ChatGPT-class tools; creative veterinary/cancer cases) are not flukes—they preview the standard. Roughly 230 million people weekly already use ChatGPT for health queries; friends and his own family rely on it to reconcile conflicting advice, read charts, and manage conditions.
- AI can empower patients, catch missed details, support rare diagnoses, aid discovery, and ease burnout in a strained system. Personalized medicine and prevention could reduce enormous economic and human burden. Applying AI to medicine is a personal motivation for him; he is confident society can make the most of it if deployed wisely.
